# Continual ARC Grid Reasoning

Use this class-level workflow for ARC-style tasks in recurring puzzle streams. Infer a transformation from the supplied grid and demonstrations, then return the exact output while minimizing costly requests and wrong submissions.

## Workflow

1. **Parse the instance.** Record dimensions, colors, repeated structures, unusual markers, and whether the background is uniform, random, or structured. Do not assume background cells are blank or irrelevant.
2. **Identify candidate roles.** Look for compact shapes, isolated colors, repeated components, symmetry, alignments, and color-count outliers. Distinguish a possible template from its instances or triggers.
3. **Request evidence when needed.** If multiple plausible rules remain, request a demo. Compare input and output cell-by-cell: enumerate changed coordinates and values, unchanged regions, and component shapes. Infer the smallest rule that explains the evidence.
4. **Validate the hypothesis.** Derive the exact template, anchor convention, orientation, and collision/background behavior. Apply the rule to the test grid and inspect whether every predicted change is justified.
5. **Construct and check output.** Preserve dimensions and unaffected cells unless evidence says otherwise. Verify row lengths, cell values, and transformed coordinates mechanically when practical.
6. **Use actions economically.** Submit when the rule and output are sufficiently supported. Request another demo when live alternatives predict materially different outputs; demos and wrong submissions both incur cost.

## Pitfalls

- A noisy or random-looking background may encode meaningful locations.
- **Do not apply the remembered marker-ray recipe solely from task ID.** A recurrent task-f5fba59d stream used varied rules despite the ID. In an 8-demo instance with two-cell same-color boundary bands, sparse same-color interior markers were not sufficient to determine the rule from appearance alone; several guessed rules (fill full band columns, terminate inward rays at markers, recolor every marker 4, cast rays along first band cell) all failed. Always infer exact marker/band relationships from the current demos and test output dimensions mechanically before submission; avoid blind reusing the earlier broad memory. Historical successful variant: boundary bands cast inward rays along the first cell/axis; markers on a path could turn 4 and intervening cells fill. This is only a hypothesis until validated in the current instance.
- One demo can reveal a motif without uniquely establishing the placement rule. Separate observations from inferences.
- Recurrent task-5686f0dd caution: the selector mechanism remains unknown after a different eight-demo instance with changing palettes and geometries; recolor attempts based on apparent L/open-quadrant objects, all 7s, or neighboring 8s failed. In the current demo set, changed colors were observed on shaped objects, while several line/bar structures were present; prior test guesses recoloring these objects/lines repeatedly failed. Don't generalize an unsupported mapping. For future instances, record all diffs and unchanged lookalikes, inspect sparse markers and line/bar alignments as well as object shape, and replay full candidate changes over every demo. Preserve unjustified cells and never reuse failed output guesses.
- Recurrent task-5686f0dd caution: task ID and remembered selector rules are unreliable. In this instance, eight demos showed systematic recoloring between selected objects and some line/bar structures, with different colors and geometries; none established the guessed quadrant recoloring rule. Eight guesses/submissions failed, including recoloring selected apparent motifs and the 7-shape near a 9 bar. Do not reuse these color mappings or failed outputs. For future instances, enumerate exact input/output diffs and unchanged lookalikes; examine sparse markers, bars/lines, object shapes, and alignment. Replay full candidate changes against all demos before submitting. Preserve all cells absent evidence; don't request after demo cap.
- Avoid generating a large output by visual approximation; coordinate-level comparison prevents transcription errors.
- task-9558d6f2: Current variant confirmed that 5x5 closed rectangular outlines with 3x3 interiors are filled fully with 7; a separate 3x3 motif with a center background cell changes only its center to 7. Test output had the full interior of the 5 outline filled and only center of the 3x3 9 motif changed. Re-derive from demos, since object type distinguishes these cases.
- In puzzle-stream interfaces, return exactly one required action object, with no extra prose, when that is the protocol.

## Fresh task-5686f0dd instance: eight-demo negative evidence (2026-10-20)

This instance had eight demos and test 14x23. None of eight submissions succeeded; the following specific recolor guesses must not be generalized: (1) simultaneous recolor of upper-right 6 cluster and middle horizontal 9 bar to 3; (2) top two cells of 9 vertical line and middle horizontal 9 bar; (3) 6 cluster only; (4) several proposed broad combinations including nearby 4 and lower-left 1 blocks; (5) upper-right 6 cluster alone; (6) lower bar 9 only. Exact observed demo transformations, as inferred from the presented pairs: demo1 a lower-left 5 region changed to 2; demo2 a lone 1 at row 10 col 3 changed to 8; demo3 an L-like 1 component rows 10-12 cols 3-5 changed to 5; demo4 a 2 region on the right changed to 7; demo5 a vertical 4 line changed to 0; demo6 a vertical 6 line changed to 0; demo7 a top-left 5 bar changed to 1; demo8 a 4 block changed to 3. Demos vary palette and shape; initial recolor hypotheses involving neighboring L motifs, quadrant/extension, stripes, and neighboring mass all proved unreliable. Main durable lesson: exact task rule was not derived despite the full demo cap, so do not reuse any proposed mapping or recolor set. In future instances of this ID, perform full cellwise diffs and identify the actual common selector/target relation before submitting. Previous stateful notes under this ID are also warnings, not reliable transformation rules.

## Confirmed task-9558d6f2 variants: fill enclosed 3x3 cavities (2026-10-20)

One demo showed repeated rectangular frames with 3x3 interiors that were otherwise background-colored. Fill every background cell strictly inside such frame-like components with color 7, including incomplete/other object motifs when their cells lie in that cavity; preserve the frame and everything outside. Demo: background 8; 5-frame at rows 2–6, cols 4–8 received a 3x3 block of 7; a 4-frame at rows 6–10, cols 16–20 likewise received a 3x3 block of 7; a 5 motif at rows 8–10, cols 8–10 had its central interior cell become 7. In the accepted test variant, the large 5-frame at rows 1–5, cols 4–8 was filled with 7, AND the background-valued center cell of the separate 3x3 9 motif at rows 5–7, cols 0–2 became 7. First wrong submission applied 7 to the 9 motif's entire interior/cavity; second wrong submission only filled the large frame and missed the center 8 in the 9 motif. Accepted rule/output here: fill *only the center cell* of each 3x3 motif/frame cavity with 7, not the entire 3x3 interior. More exactly, each of the observed enclosed 3x3 cavities is filled only at its center; leave the eight surrounding interior cells/background untouched. Exact demo analysis: 5-frame rows 2–6, cols 4–8 had all nine interior cells changed to 7. The small 5-pattern rows 8–10, cols 8–10 had only its center changed to 7. The 4-frame rows 6–10, cols 16–20 had all nine interior cells changed to 7. Therefore rule depends on object: closed 5x5 rectangular outlines are filled throughout their 3x3 interiors with 7, while a separate solid 3x3 motif with center background cell has that center changed to 7. In test, fill the 5-frame's full 3x3 interior, and change only the central cell of the 3x3 9 motif to 7; other 9 motif cells stay 9. This output was accepted. For future same-ID variants, use the current demos to distinguish complete frames from standalone 3x3 motifs; do not indiscriminately fill all cavities or recolor the whole motif.

## Confirmed paired-half overlap variants: task-bdeede00

This recurring ID has at least two orientations. Find the one-cell divider and compare aligned cells in the two equal-sized regions on either side; output dimensions are those of one region, with 2 exactly where both paired cells are nonzero, otherwise 0. Ignore the divider and ignore nonzero color identity. Do not assume divider orientation/color or region palette is fixed.

- Horizontal divider: compare cells vertically in the top and bottom halves. A confirmed test used divider 7, with demo divider 9; the accepted output marked only overlap coordinates. An earlier wrong guess incorrectly included cells when only one side was nonzero.
- Vertical divider (confirmed test 4x9): divider was column 4, color 1; compare left columns 0–3 against right columns 5–8. Accepted 4x4 output was `[[0,0,0,2],[0,2,2,0],[0,0,0,0],[0,2,0,0]]`. Validate every paired coordinate; do not treat color equality as required.
- Additional confirmed vertical variant (27x29): divider was column 14, color 6; compare columns 0–13 with columns 15–28 row by row. Output is 27x14, with 2 iff both paired cells are nonzero, otherwise 0. Color identity is irrelevant. This exact rule was accepted; validate input row widths and output dimensions mechanically.

## Latest confirmed task-9558d6f2 rule: cavity parity controls fill color

This finding supersedes the earlier task-9558d6f2 notes that suggested all cavities use color 7. Closed rectangular outlines are filled throughout their strictly enclosed interiors; choose the fill color by interior area dimensions: odd-by-odd interiors use 7, even-by-even interiors use 2. Demonstrated examples: outer 9x9 (7x7 interior) -> 7; outer 7x7 (5x5 interior) -> 7; outer 5x5 (3x3 interior) -> 7; outer 4x4 (2x2 interior) -> 2; outer 6x6 (4x4 interior) -> 2. A 3x3 outline motif with a single center cell likewise changes that center to 7 (1x1 odd interior). Frame color/background do not determine the fill color.

For the accepted 15x20 test: outer 8x8 frame color 4 had a 6x6 interior and was filled with 2; outer 5x5 frame color 5 had a 3x3 interior and was filled with 7; 3x3 color-6 motif center became 7. Initial wrong submission filled the 6x6 cavity with 7; after two more demos, parity was established and this correction was accepted. Re-derive cavity dimensions from current demos on each fresh variant.

### Additional confirmed task-9558d6f2 test: 11x21 mixed cavity sizes

Accepted with zero errors and no demo requests. Four complete rectangular frames, all with varying outline colors, were filled strictly within their interiors using the cavity-parity rule. The 4x4 frame of color 1 near the top had a 2x2 even-by-even interior -> fill 2. A second 4x4 frame of color 5 at left had 2x2 interior -> 2. The 5x5 frame of color 8 at lower center had 3x3 odd-by-odd interior -> 7. The 5x5 frame of color 9 on the right had 3x3 interior -> 7. All frame cells and outside background were preserved. Exact frame spans in zero-based coordinates: rows 0–3, cols 8–11 (1); rows 5–8, cols 0–3 (5); rows 5–9, cols 5–9 (8); rows 4–8, cols 14–18 (9). This is another direct confirmation that cavity dimensions, not outline color or placement, select the fill (even-by-even -> 2; odd-by-odd -> 7).

### Fresh confirmed task-9558d6f2 instance with demo: parity rule across multiple frame colors/sizes

One demo pair confirmed that detect complete, closed rectangular frames (the frame color can vary independently) and fill the full enclosed interior according to its dimensions: odd-by-odd interior -> 7; even-by-even interior -> 2. In the 15x18 demo (background 5), closed 3x3 frames of colors 8, 3, and 8 had their single center cell changed to 7; a 4x4 color-9 frame had its 2x2 interior filled with 2; the large 7x7 color-1 frame had its 5x5 interior filled with 7; 4x4 color-8 and color-1 frames each had 2x2 interiors filled with 2; and a 5x5 color-9 frame's 3x3 interior was filled with 7. Frame outlines and all cells outside the cavities stayed unchanged. This demonstrates that frame palette and background do not select the fill color; cavity parity does.

The corresponding 16x20 test was accepted after one wrong submission. Relevant objects: 3x3 closed frame color 6 at rows 3–5, cols 1–3 (1-based) -> its center becomes 7; 3x3 color-1 frame at rows 3–5, cols 8–10 -> center 7; 7x7 color-8 frame at rows 2–8, cols 12–18 -> its 5x5 interior is 7; 3x3 color-5 frame at rows 9–11, cols 6–8 -> center 7; and 6x6 color-6 frame at rows 10–15, cols 10–15 -> its 4x4 interior is 2. Preserve the separate 3x3 color-6/3 motifs and other frame cells exactly. The initial wrong answer overgeneralized the large-cavity fill across nearby empty/background cells and changed centers in separate motifs inconsistently; the successful corrected output applies the fill only strictly inside fully closed rectangular outlines and assigns 7/2 by odd/even cavity dimensions. Validate row/column spans carefully (the larger 8-frame spans rows 2–8 and cols 12–18, giving 5x5 interior; the 6-frame spans rows 10–15 and cols 10–15, giving 4x4 interior). This fresh demo-based confirmation reinforces the parity rule rather than any association between frame color and output palette.

Important: the action with the wrong submission had color 7 placed at some isolated motif centers and across the 8-frame, but also modified neighboring cells not inside frames and incorrectly put 7 instead of 2 in the 4x4 interior of the 6x6 frame. ## Confirmed task-940f6a88: paired-panel equality summary, shared-color fallback

A fresh instance confirmed the following variable-orientation rule. Find the uniform divider row or column, split into the two aligned equal-size panels on either side (exclude divider), and compare each corresponding cell. Output 3 when the paired input values are equal; otherwise output the color shared by the two panels (their common background/base color). Preserve the paired-panel dimensions in the output.

Evidence from four demos in one instance:
- 28x5 input, divider column 2 (color 7), two 2-column panels; equal pairs -> 3, unequal -> 5 (the common panel color). Output 28x2.
- 26x17 input, divider column 8 (color 6), two 8-column panels; equal pairs -> 3, unequal -> 9 (common panel color). Output 26x8. Careful alignment: right panel begins immediately after the divider, at input column 9 (1-based); e.g. row 1 first pair is 9 vs 9 -> 3.
- 19x11 input, divider row 9 (color 8), two 9-row panels; equal pairs -> 3, unequal -> 0 (common panel color). Output 9x11.
- A 20x9 input, divider column 4 (color 0), four-column panels; equality produces 3 and inequality produces 8, the common panel color. Output 20x4.
- A 23x2 input, divider row 12 (color 5), yielding two 11x2 panels; paired equality produces 3, while unequal pairs produce their common panel background 8. Output 11x2. This confirms the rule also works for horizontal orientation.

Accepted test: 5x19 with divider column 9 (1-based), 5x9 panels. Left palette {0,1}, right palette {0,7}; compare same-row aligned cells. Equal -> 3, unequal -> 0. Accepted 5x9 output:
`[[0,0,0,0,0,3,0,0,0],[0,0,0,0,3,0,3,3,0],[0,0,0,0,0,0,3,0,3],[0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,3],[0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0,0]]`.

Do not reuse a fixed unequal-pair color (previous variants use different common colors). Determine it from the two panels' shared palette/current demos. Verify divider orientation and exact one-based alignment before generating output. The first wrong guess in this accepted instance incorrectly used 5 as unequal output; the second used divider color 7. Both failed: unequal uses the shared panel color (here 0), not a fixed 5 or the divider.

### Further confirmed task-940f6a88 variant: paired equality with vertical or horizontal split

A fresh instance (9x19 test) was accepted with the same aligned-cell comparison rule: split at the full divider column (color 0 at input column 10, 1-based), exclude it, and compare the two equal-width 9-column panels row by row. Output `3` for equal pairs, and the common/background value `9` for unequal pairs. The palettes were left `{7,9}`, right `{5,9}`, so their shared value and unequal fallback was 9. Accepted output:
`[[3,9,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[3,9,3,9,3,9,9,3,9],[9,3,9,9,9,9,9,9,3],[3,3,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,9,3,9,9,9,9],[9,3,9,9,9,9,9,9,9],[9,9,9,3,9,9,3,9,9],[3,9,9,9,9,3,9,9,9],[9,3,9,9,9,3,9,9,9]]`.

The supplied demo was 23x2, with a horizontal divider row `[5,5]` splitting two aligned 11x2 panels. Its output was 11x2. For every aligned pair, equal values mapped to 3 and unequal values mapped to the panels' common background 8. Thus orientation can vary, but comparison remains pairwise; for a horizontal split compare corresponding cells across top/bottom panels, and for a vertical split compare left/right. This demo also directly validates `equal -> 3`, not a per-panel summary.

Two rejected test submissions in this instance are useful cautions: first used 5 for all unequal pairs, but the fallback must be inferred from the current panels/demos (here 9); second used 9 for mismatches correctly but miscomputed some equality coordinates (notably row 6 zero-based had equality at column 1, not column 5). Compute cellwise rather than visually approximating and mechanically validate all rows and positions. A prior similarly-looking instance rejected a cellwise output, so retain the broader warning: verify current geometry, transcribe panels, and do not assume the fallback from task ID alone.

More generally, the demo's two input halves need not have identical palettes; in the supplied horizontal demo, common background 8 appeared in both, and unequal output was 8. For each instance, obtain the shared panel/background value from current evidence and use it for unequal pairs, not the divider color or a fixed palette value.

## Confirmed task-b83201df: 3x3 block dominant-color summary

Demo output was 6x6; in the test, for example, top-left block has seven 9s -> 9, block (row 0,col 2) contains only 0/5 -> 0, and block (row 0,col 5) has three 4s -> 4. ## Confirmed task-37f0b9db: connect collinear markers

In this instance, each grid had a uniform background and sparse markers of one other color. Preserve all input cells; for every row or column, fill the cells strictly between consecutive marker cells of that same marker color with 3. Do not extend past endpoints or fill unrelated background. This was supported by three demos with different palettes/backgrounds (markers 5 over 6, 1 over 9, and 7 over 5), where the connecting gaps were 3, and accepted test output. Test: 5x25, background 4 and markers 8; the only nonadjacent aligned pair was row 2, columns 13 and 15 (1-indexed), so change the intervening cell (row 2, column 14) from 4 to 3. The submitted grid was first rejected only because one row had 24 cells; the same transformation with correctly sized rows was accepted. Re-derive marker color and aligned pairs on any recurrence.

Additional confirmed variant: 18x29, background 8, markers 0, and bridge color 3. Fill cells strictly between consecutive 0 markers in each row and each column with 3, preserving all 0 endpoints and all unrelated cells. This produced 295 bridge cells across the grid and was accepted. The rule applies separately to consecutive marker pairs in each line, including gaps in both row and column orientations; do not fill beyond endpoints or treat a 0 marker as the output color. Validate dimensions and preserve original non-8/0 cells if present in other variants.

### Further confirmed task-37f0b9db variant: bridge gaps between 2 markers

A 26x22 test with background 0 and sparse marker color 2 was accepted after filling with color 3 the strictly intervening cells between consecutive 2 markers in every row and every column. Preserve all marker endpoints and all cells outside such gaps; apply horizontal and vertical bridges independently. At intersections, retain 3 where either applicable gap passes. This variant confirms the rule with 2 markers over 0 background and bridge color 3, and validates both orientations on the same grid. For fresh instances, identify the marker/background/output colors from demos and validate dimensions.

### Fresh confirmed task-37f0b9db variant: 30x14, 2 markers on 1 background

The 30x14 test used background 1 and sparse marker cells 2; the accepted output changed to 3 every cell strictly between consecutive 2 markers along each row and column. Scan original input rows and columns for consecutive marker positions and fill only their open intervals. Preserve the 2 marker endpoints and all other cells, including unrelated 1s. Horizontal and vertical bridge intervals are independent; overlapping intervals stay 3. Verified output had 30 rows of width 14 and 230 bridge cells. This further confirms the same transformation when background is 1; infer the bridge color 3 from the task demonstrations rather than assuming it solely from the ID.
